description: Solve Continual-ARC instances by reusing task programs, inferring grid transforms from demonstrations, and validating submissions.

# Continual ARC

Use this procedure for task-id grid puzzles with an available program library.

1. For every reply in an instance, output only one supported action as a JSON object on the last line; omit commentary. Check `programs/<task id>.py`; if present, run `transform(grid)` on the test input and submit that exact output before requesting demos. After a wrong verdict, do not retry the same output; use the demo-and-repair loop below.
2. Infer the transformation jointly from all demos. Request a demo only if its possible outcomes distinguish plausible rules; weigh its cost against remaining attempts and demo allowance.
3. Implement or repair a candidate, then execute it on the test and every received input-output pair. Require exact shape and cell-by-cell agreement with all pairs before submission; submit only the checked program output, not a manually guessed grid. Keep the prior library file intact until a candidate passes every demo; if none does, leave the library file unchanged. After a wrong verdict, treat it only as evidence the current rule is wrong—not as localization or confirmation of particular cells—and revisit all demos before changing the rule. A demo-matching heuristic is not established merely because one candidate matches; test alternate hypotheses against the full examples and request a discriminating demo when the unresolved distinction could change the test output.
4. Once the transformation is supported by every demo, prefer another discriminating demo over speculative submissions when uncertainty remains. Do not claim verification if demo agreement is incomplete.
5. After a correct verdict, save the verified transform at `programs/<task id>.py`, replacing any older version, then finish.

Validate parsing and panel geometry explicitly: locate all dividers, including repeated vertical and horizontal lines of any color; determine panel bounds and orientation from their positions, not from global color frequency. Derive panel background/foreground from evidence. When outputs encode per-panel features, calculate those features panel-by-panel and confirm their mapping (including thresholds and output colors) against every demo before encoding it. Check whether the output represents an overlay, comparison, or another relation; avoid hardcoded colors or guessed majority rules unless demos establish them.

Each instance has its own attempt and demo costs. Feedback on a submission is only correct/incorrect, so use it to trigger hypothesis revision, not as a cell-level diagnosis.

def transform(grid):
    h, w = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    hs = [r for r,row in enumerate(grid) if all(v == row[0] for v in row)]
    vs = [c for c in range(w) if all(grid[r][c] == grid[0][c] for r in range(h))]
    rb, cb = [-1] + hs + [h], [-1] + vs + [w]
    # Each 3x3 panel has a distinctive marker color among its background.
    # Mark panel 1 when its marker appears, otherwise background color.
    out = []
    for i in range(len(rb)-1):
        row = []
        for j in range(len(cb)-1):
            vals = [grid[r][c] for r in range(rb[i]+1, rb[i+1]) for c in range(cb[j]+1, cb[j+1])]
            # Background is the most frequent tile color; marker is the remaining
            # non-divider color. A marker count of two or more maps to 1.
            bg = max(set(vals), key=vals.count)
            markers = [v for v in set(vals) if v != bg]
            marker = markers[0] if markers else None
            row.append(1 if marker is not None and vals.count(marker) >= 2 else bg)
        out.append(row)
    return out
